problem: Prior assistive robots for visually impaired users mostly do obstacle avoidance and point-to-point navigation, and existing object-search methods handle single objects. Multi-object methods like Finder always go to frontiers, so they cannot revisit regions to recover from missed detections or occlusions.
motivation: Retrieving several objects in cluttered indoor spaces is cognitively demanding and common in daily life for blind or visually impaired people. Purely greedy, frontier-only value-map search abandons promising regions where a target was occluded, which motivates belief-space planning with revisiting.
key_idea: Combine a VLM multi-layer value map with a POUCT-solved POMDP whose actions are DBSCAN candidate points from a decayed value map plus the best frontier, allowing revisits of high-value regions and trading off exploration against exploitation.
insight: Ablations show both parts matter: removing POMDP planning drops SR from 55.0% to 27.5%, because greedy selection ignores travel cost and the explore/exploit trade-off. Removing value decay drops SR to 45.0%, because the robot gets stuck on misleading high-value regions. Qualitatively, revisiting high-value areas finds occluded objects (a toilet in a corner, an umbrella behind a trash can) that Finder misses.
method: Multi-layer value map: BLIP-2 cosine similarity between RGB and per-target text prompts, with FOV cone confidence weighting and confidence-weighted temporal averaging; per-object maps are normalized and aggregated assuming independence (product of beliefs).
Object map: Grounding DINO, YOLOv7 and SAM detect, segment and store objects during search.
Obstacle and frontier maps: top-down 2D obstacle map from depth and odometry; frontier midpoints extracted; the highest-value frontier is chosen as the exploratory point.

Value decay and candidate points: sigmoid decay over per-cell update count, thresholding, then DBSCAN clustering into candidate points forming the action space MoveTo(candidates) plus MoveTo(frontier).

OO-POMDP planner: belief is a discrete distribution over candidate points; reward = -move cost + frontier bonus + target proximity bonus; observation model is binary detection with exponential decay in distance; solved with POUCT. Real-world belief update is approximated by the decayed value map.
Navigation controller: converts the MoveTo target to discrete forward/turn-left/turn-right commands on the GuideBot (TurtleBot 2, ZED camera, handlebar).

setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (ZED stereo camera) with odometry
setting.action_space: discrete forward / turn left / turn right, driven by high-level MoveTo candidate or frontier points

numbers_note: Simulation baselines (Random 0.0/0.0, VLFM 12.5%/0.075, Finder 28.3%/0.198) are in Table 1 but excluded as baselines. Real-world tables count success per trial; the discussion also reports 54.2% end-to-end (26/48).
results: In simulation on 120 HM3D multi-object episodes, OpenGuide reaches 55.0% SR and 0.497 MSPL versus Finder's 28.3% and 0.198, about double the SR. Real-world success is 50.0% in a home and 56.7% in an office, with 54.2% end-to-end over 48 trials.
limitations: Detection pipeline struggles with small, occluded or ambiguous objects (11 of 16 search failures), and robot sometimes stops too far from the target (5 failures).
Real-world evaluation is small (48 trials, two environments), the simulation set is only 120 episodes in 5 scenes, and no user study with visually impaired people is reported.
Navigation failures from SLAM collisions and getting trapped in narrow spaces; success only about 55%.
